title: The Universe Outruns Light — Without Breaking Einstein
hook: Galaxies far enough away recede from us faster than light, and relativity is fine with it. The catch: accelerating expansion is slowly emptying our sky.
key_points: Cosmic expansion lets distant galaxies move away from us faster than light.
Nothing is racing through space — space itself is stretching, so no speed limit is broken.
We still see their ancient light: it left when those galaxies were far closer to us.
Accelerating expansion will push nearly everything beyond our Local Group out of view.
Far-future astronomers would inherit a sky that looks almost empty.
content_html: Some galaxies are receding from us faster than light. That sounds like a flat violation of Einstein, and it isn't: relativity limits how fast anything can travel through space, and those galaxies aren't traveling anywhere. Space itself is stretching between us and them, and stretching has no speed limit.
extra_html: The stranger part, as this ScienceDaily report lays out, is that we can still see galaxies that now outrun light. The photons reaching our telescopes tonight left when those galaxies were far closer, so what we observe is a snapshot of their distant past rather than their present. But the arrangement is temporary. Because the expansion is accelerating, more and more of the sky is being carried past the point where its light can ever reach us. Eventually almost everything outside our own gravitationally bound Local Group will slip out of view, leaving future astronomers with a universe that looks nearly empty — and very hard to figure out.

flashcards.prompt: Why doesn't faster-than-light recession of distant galaxies violate relativity?

choices.text: They aren't moving through space — the space between us is stretching
Relativity's speed limit only applies to massless particles
The galaxies are so far away the limit no longer applies

flashcards.explanation_html: Relativity caps how fast anything can move through space past you. Cosmic expansion stretches space itself, so the recession speed it produces has no such ceiling.

flashcards.prompt: If a galaxy now recedes faster than light, how can we still see it?
flashcards.back_html: The light we're receiving left long ago, when that galaxy was much closer to us. We see its ancient past, not the galaxy as it is today.

flashcards.prompt: What does accelerating expansion imply for the far-future night sky?

choices.text: Nearly everything outside our Local Group drifts out of sight
Galaxies crowd together as the universe contracts
The sky brightens as more distant light finally arrives

flashcards.explanation_html: As expansion accelerates, galaxies beyond our gravitationally bound Local Group are carried out of view — leaving a universe that looks almost empty from the inside.
